title: Create a Summer Barbecue Skewers with Thin Bell Pepper
meta_description: Master the art of summer grilling with these thin-slice bell pepper skewers. Learn how to use a mandoline for perfect, restaurant-style veggie ribbons.
html:
There is a common frustration when grilling vegetables: some pieces are charred to a crisp while others remain raw in the center. This usually happens because of uneven thickness. When you're prepping for a crowd, hand-chopping a dozen bell peppers into perfectly uniform strips is tedious and often imprecise. That is why I swear by using mandoline bell pepper skewers to get that professional, consistent cook every single time.

By slicing your peppers thin, you create a larger surface area for caramelization. Instead of a chunky piece of pepper that takes ten minutes to soften, a thin ribbon blisters and sweetens in a fraction of the time, wrapping perfectly around proteins or other vegetables on the skewer.

The Secret to Perfect Mandoline Bell Pepper Skewers

The goal here isn't just "thin"—it's consistent. When you use a Mandoline Slicer, you can set the blade to a precise thickness that ensures every single piece of pepper hits the grill grate at the same angle. This prevents the "burnt edge/raw middle" syndrome.

To get the best results, slice your bell peppers lengthwise. This creates long, elegant strips that can be folded or spiraled around the skewer. If you are pairing the peppers with shrimp or scallops, a thinner slice is better so the pepper doesn't outlast the delicate protein. For heartier options like steak or halloumi, you can bump the thickness up slightly using the adjustable settings on your Mandoline Slicer.

Step-by-Step: Prepping Your Summer Skewers

Before you start slicing, make sure your peppers are washed and the seeds are removed. I prefer to cut the top and bottom off the pepper and slice the skin away in four large quadrants. This gives you a flat surface to glide across the blade.

Follow these steps for the most efficient prep:

  • Safety First: Always use the hand guard provided with your Mandoline Slicer. As the pepper gets smaller, your fingers get closer to the blade; the guard is non-negotiable for kitchen safety.
  • Set Your Thickness: For these skewers, I recommend a setting between 1/8 and 1/4 inch. This is thin enough to char quickly but thick enough to hold its structure on the heat.
  • The Slide: Glide the pepper quadrant firmly across the blade to create uniform strips.
  • The Marinate: Toss your thin slices in a bowl with olive oil, lemon juice, garlic powder, and a pinch of smoked paprika. Because the slices are thin, they absorb the marinade much faster than chunks.

Assembling for Maximum Flavor

Now that you have your restaurant-thin slices, the assembly is where you can get creative. Instead of just sliding a flat piece of pepper onto the stick, try "weaving" them. Fold the thin strip of bell pepper back and forth, creating a ruffle. This creates little pockets that trap the marinade and grill juices.

I love pairing these with red onion (also sliced thin on the mandoline) and cubes of feta or chunks of pineapple. If you're using wooden skewers, remember to soak them in water for at least 30 minutes to prevent them from catching fire. Metal skewers are a great alternative if you have them.

Grilling Tips for Thin-Slice Veggies

Because these peppers are sliced thin, your grill time will be significantly shorter than a traditional kebab. You aren't looking to "cook" them so much as "blister" them. Keep your grill on medium-high heat.

Place the skewers on the hottest part of the grate. Give them about 2-3 minutes per side. You'll know they are done when the edges of the peppers start to turn a deep brown and the proteins are cooked through. If you leave them too long, the thin slices will disintegrate, so stay vigilant and keep them moving.

Cleaning and Maintenance

After you've finished prepping your feast, don't let the vegetables dry on your equipment. The Mandoline Slicer is a powerhouse, but the blades stay sharpest when they are kept clean. Rinse the blade and the hand guard immediately after use with warm, soapy water. Avoid using abrasive scrubbers on the blade to maintain that razor-sharp edge for your next summer cookout.

FAQ

Can I use a mandoline for other skewer vegetables?

Absolutely. Zucchini, carrots, and red onions all benefit from the precision of a mandoline. Just be mindful that carrots are denser, so you may want a slightly thicker slice than you would use for a bell pepper.

What is the best way to stop the peppers from slipping off the skewer?

The "fold method" is key. By folding your thin slices over themselves, you create more points of contact with the skewer, which locks the vegetable in place and prevents it from sliding off during the flip.

Do I need to peel the bell peppers first?

No, there is no need to peel them. The skin is where a lot of the flavor and structure live. The high heat of the grill will soften the skin and create those delicious charred spots that make barbecue skewers so tasty.
